(CNN) — President Obama delivered the commencement address Friday to the graduating class of the U.S. Naval Academy, speaking before an audience of 30,000 that included a former presidential candidate and proud parent of one of the graduates.

Jack McCain shook hands with President Obama at Friday’s commencement ceremony.

John Sidney McCain IV, more commonly known as Jack, became on Friday the fourth McCain to graduate from the service academy in Annapolis, Maryland, and the fourth to bear the same name.

“America, look at these young men and women. Look at these sailors and Marines. Here are the values that we cherish. Here are the ideals that endure,” Obama told the crowd.

Around midday, during the academy’s commissioning and graduation ceremony, McCain received a Bachelor of Science degree, took the oath of office, and was commissioned as an ensign in the U.S. Navy—103 years after his great-grandfather did the same.

Watch Obama hug John McCain’s son »

With his parents, John and Cindy McCain, looking on, he shook hands with the president and then returned to the crowd to applause and more hugs.

Joe McCain told CNN that his brother plans to follow his father and great-grandfather in becoming a naval aviator.

“His grandfather, JSM Jr., was in submarines, commanding three different boats in World War II,” he said.

That grandfather later became Adm. McCain and served as commander of the Pacific Theater during the Vietnam War, when Jack’s father, now Arizona Sen. John McCain, was being held as a prisoner of war in Hanoi.

In an interview last year with GoMids.com, Jack McCain reflected on the advice his father gave him on the day he arrived at the Naval Academy.

“My dad told me there is one thing McCains are good at, and that is not giving in to pressure, and honor—keeping our honor regardless of what happens,” Jack McCain said. “He then said, ‘Don’t lie, cheat or steal—anything else is fair game.’”

John McCain, the Republican presidential nominee in 2008, frequently made light of his own record at the Naval Academy while on the campaign trail, noting that he “stood fifth from the bottom” of his class and had accumulated dozens of demerits.

At a campaign event last October, McCain joked that Jack needed a “DNA check” because he had not yet received a single demerit. Jack McCain told GoMids.com that he did, in fact, accumulate some demerits—for wearing flip-flops outside and forgetting to shave.

McCain told Fox News on Thursday that his son was graduating “in better class standing than I had, which wasn’t hard to do.”

“I’m very proud of him,” he said.

Meghan McCain, Jack’s older sister, posted a message on Twitter Friday saying that her younger brother, Jimmy, could not attend because he was serving overseas. McCain told Fox News that Jimmy is returning home this weekend.

In his remarks to the students, Obama pledged that he would not send them to war unless it was “absolutely necessary.”

“It’s a promise that as long as I am your commander in chief, I will only send you into harm’s way when it is absolutely necessary, and with the strategy, the well-defined goals, the equipment and the support that you need to get the job done,” he said. “This includes the job of bringing the Iraq war to a responsible end and pursuing a new comprehensive strategy to disrupt, dismantle and defeat al Qaeda and its allies in Afghanistan and Pakistan.”

Obama also promised additional assistance to military families, pledging that “we will be with you every step of the way, increasing your pay, increasing child care and helping families deal with the stress and separation of war.”

He added that new laws would help ensure that veterans are well cared for.

Obama’s commencement address was his third and final such speech of the year. He had also served as commencement speaker at Arizona State University and the University of Notre Dame.

“America, look at these young men and women. Look at these sailors and Marines. Here are the values that we cherish. Here are the ideals that endure,” Obama said to the audience.

With his parents, John and Cindy McCain, looking on, Jack shook the president’s hand before returning to the crowd, where he was greeted with applause and hugs.

Joe McCain told CNN that his brother intends to follow in the footsteps of both his father and great-grandfather by becoming a naval aviator. He noted that Jack’s grandfather, JSM Jr., served in submarines and commanded three different vessels during World War II.

That grandfather later became Admiral McCain and went on to command the Pacific Theater during the Vietnam War, the same period when Jack’s father — now Arizona Sen. John McCain — was being held as a prisoner of war in Hanoi.

In a 2008 interview with GoMids.com, Jack McCain recalled the guidance his father offered when he first arrived at the Naval Academy.

“My dad told me there is one thing McCains are good at, and that is not giving in to pressure, and honor — keeping our honor regardless of what happens,” Jack said. “He then said, ‘Don’t lie, cheat or steal — anything else is fair game.’”

John McCain, the Republican nominee for president in 2008, often joked during the campaign about his own Naval Academy record. He liked to point out that he graduated “fifth from the bottom” of his class and collected dozens of demerits.

At a campaign appearance the previous October, McCain quipped that Jack might need a “DNA check” because he had not yet received even one demerit. Jack later told GoMids.com that he had, in fact, earned some — including for wearing flip-flops outdoors and failing to shave.

Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, McCain said his son was graduating “in better class standing than I had, which wasn’t hard to do.”

“I’m very proud of him,” he added.

Meghan McCain, Jack’s older sister, posted on Twitter Friday that their younger brother, Jimmy, was unable to attend because he was serving overseas. McCain told Fox News that Jimmy would be coming home that weekend.

In his speech to the midshipmen, Obama pledged that he would not send them into combat unless doing so was “absolutely necessary.”

“It’s a promise that as long as I am your commander in chief, I will only send you into harm’s way when it is absolutely necessary, and with the strategy, the well-defined goals, the equipment and the support that you need to get the job done,” Obama said.

He said that mission included “bringing the Iraq war to a responsible end” and carrying out a broader new strategy “to disrupt, dismantle and defeat al Qaeda and its allies in Afghanistan and Pakistan.”

Obama also committed to providing more support for military families. He promised that “we will be with you every step of the way,” including by raising pay, expanding child care and helping families cope with the strain and separation caused by war.

He also said that new laws would help make sure veterans receive proper care.

The Naval Academy speech was Obama’s third and final commencement address of the year. Earlier, he had delivered commencement remarks at Arizona State University and the University of Notre Dame.

**ANNAPOLIS, Md., May 22, 2009** — President Barack Obama delivered his first commencement address as commander in chief Friday at the United States Naval Academy, telling the graduating class that they were entering military service at a time of war and would be asked to lead with discipline, humility and moral purpose.

Among the newly commissioned officers was **John “Jack” McCain**, son of Sen. John McCain of Arizona, the 2008 Republican presidential nominee and a former Navy pilot who was held as a prisoner of war in Vietnam. Jack McCain’s graduation continued one of the most prominent naval traditions in American public life: the McCain family’s multigenerational service in the Navy.

Obama, who had defeated Sen. McCain in the previous year’s presidential election, acknowledged the weight of such service and the sacrifices borne not only by those in uniform but also by their families. Speaking to the midshipmen assembled at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, the president said the nation had a duty to ensure that troops were sent into harm’s way only when necessary and that they and their families received support worthy of their service.

“You will be called upon to carry forward a tradition of honor and excellence,” Obama told the graduates, noting that many would soon serve in combat zones or aboard ships supporting operations around the world.

The Class of 2009 graduated at a pivotal moment for the U.S. military. American forces remained heavily engaged in **Iraq**, while the Obama administration was increasing its focus on the war in **Afghanistan**, which the president had described as central to confronting al-Qaida and extremist networks. Obama used the address to frame the conflicts as tests not only of military power but of national character.

He told the graduates that the United States must remain strong, but that strength should be matched by adherence to American ideals. He emphasized that America’s military power was most effective when joined with diplomacy, alliances, development and the example of lawful conduct.

Obama also spoke directly about the human cost of war. He praised the resilience of military spouses, parents and children, saying they serve in their own way through long deployments, uncertainty and loss. The president pledged that his administration would work to improve care for wounded warriors, support veterans returning home and strengthen assistance for military families.

The presence of Jack McCain underscored the generational nature of that service. His father, Sen. McCain, graduated from the Naval Academy in 1958 before becoming a naval aviator. Shot down over Hanoi in 1967, he spent more than five years as a prisoner of war. Jack McCain’s grandfather, **Adm. John S. McCain Jr.**, was a World War II submarine commander and later commander in chief of U.S. Pacific Command during the Vietnam War. His great-grandfather, **Adm. John S. McCain Sr.**, was a carrier task force commander in World War II. Both elder McCains became four-star admirals, making the family one of the Navy’s most storied lineages.

Although the 2008 campaign had been hard fought, Obama’s appearance at the Naval Academy served as a reminder of the continuity of military service beyond partisan politics. Sen. Obama told the graduates that they would face enemies who do not follow the rules of war and crises that cannot be solved by force alone. He urged them to uphold the values they had learned at Annapolis, including integrity, accountability and respect for the chain of command.

The president’s message blended tribute and warning: the nation was proud of its newest officers, he said, but it would ask much of them. In return, he said, the country must remain committed to those who serve.

“For you and your families, service is not an abstraction,” Obama said in substance. “It is a lived commitment — one that carries sacrifice, responsibility and honor.”

The graduates, commissioned as ensigns in the Navy and second lieutenants in the Marine Corps, tossed their covers into the air at the end of the ceremony, marking both the conclusion of their Academy years and the beginning of military careers shaped by ongoing wars and evolving global threats.
